```{r load_emergence, include = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
emergence <- read.csv("../../../data/okanagan_sockeye_data/data_clean/fry_emergence.csv")

emergence_2024 <- read_excel("../data/Emerg data 2024 updated 2024.06.05.xlsx", sheet = "Data") |> 
  clean_names()

names(emergence_2024)

emergence_2024 <- emergence_2024 |> 
  filter(!is.na(total_sk_fry)) |> 
  select(date, set, time_set, soak_time_min = soak_time_minutes, total_catch = total_sk_fry, volume_m3, comments, meter_reading_start, meter_reading_end) |> 
  mutate(sample_year = year(date), brood_year = year(date)-1) |> 
  mutate(time_set = format(time_set, "%H:%M:%S"))

emergence_2025 <- read_excel("../data/Emerg data 2025 - recd May21_AO - wkg.xlsx", sheet = "Data") |> 
  clean_names()

names(emergence_2025)

emergence_2025 <- emergence_2025 |> 
  filter(!is.na(total_sk_fry)) |> 
  select(date, set, time_set, soak_time_min = soak_time_minutes, total_catch = total_sk_fry, volume_m3, comments, meter_reading_start, meter_reading_end) |> 
  mutate(sample_year = year(date), brood_year = year(date)-1) |> 
  mutate(time_set = format(time_set, "%H:%M:%S"))

emergence_2026 <- read_excel("../data/Emerg data 2026.xlsx", sheet = "Data") |> 
  clean_names()

names(emergence_2026)

emergence_2026 <- emergence_2026 |> 
  filter(!is.na(total_sk_fry)) |> 
  select(date, set, time_set, soak_time_min = soak_time_minutes, total_catch = total_sk_fry, volume_m3, comments, meter_reading_start, meter_reading_end) |> 
  mutate(sample_year = year(date), brood_year = year(date)-1) |> 
  mutate(time_set = format(time_set, "%H:%M:%S"))

emergence <- bind_rows(emergence |> mutate(date = as.Date(date), time_set = time_set), emergence_2024, emergence_2025)#, emergence_2026)

emergence$yday <- yday(emergence$date)

emergence$time_set_numeric <- with(emergence, {
  hours <- as.numeric(substr(time_set, 1, 2))
  minutes <- as.numeric(substr(time_set, 4, 5)) / 60
  adjusted_hours <- ifelse(hours < 10, hours + 24, hours)  # Add 24 if after midnight
  (adjusted_hours + minutes) - 20
})

ggplot(emergence, aes(x = sample_year, y = time_set_numeric))+
  geom_jitter(width = 0.25, height = 0)

emergence <- emergence %>% mutate(volume_m3 = ifelse(volume_m3<0, NA, volume_m3),
                                  mean_nightly_discharge_cms = ifelse(mean_nightly_discharge_cms>100, NA, mean_nightly_discharge_cms)) %>% 
  mutate(total_catch = as.integer(total_catch)) |> 
  filter(sample_year>2003) #|>  #2002 was the first year of sampling and methods were not yet worked out, 2003 only sampled early and late in the evening, likely missing peak emergence
  #filter(sample_year!=2018)
  
exclude_gear <- c(
  "lost a side of the fyke net frame",
  "mended hole found",
  "hole",
  "net had collapsed",
  "net got caught on itself",
  "net got caught on bank",
  "net twisted",
  "cod end caught on weight",
  "cod end twisted",
  "twisted",
  "stuck in neck",
  "switched to old net",
  "branch caught in net",
  "branch caught",
  "caught on rope",
  "caught on bank",
  "caught on weight",
  "tree caught on rope",
  "not submerged",
  "net was not set right",
  "net not set properly",
  "might not have set properly",
  "set without weights",
  "walk net out to set",
  "cod-end may have been twisted",
  "cod end might have twisted")

exclude_measurement <- c(
  "velocity conversion",
  "error in meter readings",
  "meter reading incorect",
  "meter readings were nonsense",
  "end meter reading is questionable",
  "props not working",
  "volume is average of other",
  "not submerged",
  "substituted",
  "average of other volumes",
  "meter not set properly",
  "problem with the meter",
  "velocity meter had no water",
  "velocity meter low on water",
  "debris caught in velocity metre",
  "low meter reading",
  "forgot to put velocity meter",
  "velocity meter broke",
  "reading might not be correct")


make_regex <- function(phrases) {
  parts <- phrases |>
    tolower() |>
    stringr::str_replace_all("\\s+", "\\\\s+") |>
    stringr::str_replace_all("\\(", "\\\\(") |>
    stringr::str_replace_all("\\)", "\\\\)")
  paste0("(", paste0(parts, collapse = "|"), ")")
}

gear_rx  <- make_regex(exclude_gear)
meas_rx  <- make_regex(exclude_measurement)

emergence_tagged <- emergence %>%
  mutate(
    comment_norm = if_else(is.na(comments), NA_character_, str_squish(tolower(comments))),
    gear_issue   = if_else(is.na(comment_norm), FALSE, str_detect(comment_norm, gear_rx)),
    meas_issue   = if_else(is.na(comment_norm), FALSE, str_detect(comment_norm, meas_rx))
  )

emergence_no_gear <- emergence_tagged %>% filter(!gear_issue)

emergence_no_gear <- emergence_no_gear %>%
  mutate(volume_m3 = if_else(meas_issue, NA_real_, volume_m3))



emergence_select <- emergence_no_gear %>% select(date, brood_year, sample_year, total_catch, soak_time_min, yday, time_set_numeric, volume_m3, comments) %>% 
  mutate(date = as.Date(date)) %>% 
  filter(time_set_numeric >= 1, time_set_numeric<=5) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(total_catch)) |> 
  filter(soak_time_min >=5, soak_time_min<=20, volume_m3 > 10 | is.na(volume_m3)) |> 
  filter(!(brood_year == 2010 & yday == 107 & time_set_numeric < 3)) |>  #note says "bouy not hooked up right! in sets 1-3"
  filter(!(brood_year == 2014 & yday == 118 & time_set_numeric == 2)) #no note, but almost surely an error as it has only one fish and all other sets on evening have hundreds

```{r thermal_units, include = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
temperature <- read.csv("../../../data/okanagan_sockeye_data/data_clean/ok_river_mean_daily_temperatures.csv")
#tabyl(temperature, location)
temperature$date <- as.Date(temperature$date)

temperature2 <- read.csv("../../ok_watertemp/data/oliver_air_water_temp_data.csv")
temperature2$date <- as.Date(temperature2$date)

temperature <- temperature %>% 
  select(date, temp = water_temperature_c, location) %>% 
  bind_rows(temperature2 %>% select(date, temp = mean_water_temp) %>% mutate(location = "Oliver2"))

# ggplot(temperature, aes(x = yday(date), y = temp))+
#   geom_line(aes(color = location))+
#   facet_wrap(~year(date))

temp_means <- temperature %>% 
  filter(!(location == "Okanagan River near Oliver, BC" & date >= as.Date("2007-06-01") & date <= as.Date("2008-05-30"))) %>% 
  group_by(date) %>% 
  summarise(temperature = mean(temp,na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(temp_means, aes(x = yday(date), y = temperature))+
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(100, 319))+
  geom_line()+
  facet_wrap(~year(date))

incubation_start_full <- as.Date("2025-10-12")
incubation_end_full <- as.Date("2025-04-10")

incubation_start <- format(incubation_start_full, "%B ") %>%
  paste0(as.integer(format(incubation_start_full, "%d")))

incubation_end <- format(incubation_end_full, "%B ") %>%
  paste0(as.integer(format(incubation_end_full, "%d")))

ATU.df <- temp_means %>% 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) |> 
  filter(yday <= 200 | yday > yday(incubation_start_full)) |> 
  mutate(year_start = if_else(format(date, "%m-%d") >= format(incubation_start_full, "%m-%d"),
                              year(date),
                              year(date) - 1)) %>% 
  group_by(year_start) %>% 
  arrange(date, .by_group = TRUE) %>% 
  mutate(ATU = cumsum(temperature)) %>% 
  ungroup()

ggplot(ATU.df, aes(x = yday(date), y = ATU, color = factor(year_start)))+
  geom_path()

ATU_day100 <- ATU.df %>% 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) %>% 
  mutate(year = year(date)) %>%
  filter(yday == yday(incubation_end_full))

temp_means <- temp_means |> 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) |> 
  mutate(year = year(date)) |> 
  mutate(incubation = yday < yday(incubation_end_full) | yday > yday(incubation_start_full))
```

```{r moon, include = FALSE}
ATU_emergence_thresh <- 900

new_moons <- data.frame()
for(i in 1:length(unique(emergence$sample_year))){
  year_select <- unique(emergence$sample_year)[i]
  ATU_year <- ATU.df |> filter(year_start == (year_select - 1))
  
  ATU_thresh_date <- ATU_year |> 
    filter(ATU > ATU_emergence_thresh) |> 
    slice(1)   # safer than first()
  
  start_date <- NA  # <-- important
  
  if(nrow(ATU_thresh_date) > 0 && !is.na(ATU_thresh_date$date)){
    start_date <- ATU_thresh_date$date
  }
  
  if(!is.na(start_date)){
    dates <- seq(start_date, start_date + 29, by = "day")
    new_moon_date <- dates[which.min(lunar.illumination(dates))]
    
    new_moons <- bind_rows(
      new_moons,
      data.frame(
        year = year_select,
        ATU_yday = yday(start_date),
        new_moon_date = new_moon_date,
        new_moon_yday = yday(new_moon_date)
      )
    )
  }
}

env.df <- left_join(data.frame(year = unique(emergence_select$sample_year)),new_moons) %>% 
  left_join(ATU_day100 %>% select(year, ATU))

ggplot(env.df, aes(x = new_moon_yday, y = ATU_yday))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = year))

summary(lm(ATU ~ new_moon_yday, data = env.df))
```

```{r flow, include=FALSE}
#download here - https://wateroffice.ec.gc.ca/report/data_availability_e.html?type=historical&station=08NM085&parameter_type=Flow+and+Level
flows <- read.csv("../data/flow_20260309T1903.csv", skip = 1) |> 
  clean_names() |> 
  filter(param == 1)

ggplot(flows, aes(x = date, y = value))+
  geom_line()

flow <- flows |>  
  mutate(date = as.Date(date), yday = yday(date), year = year(date)) %>% 
  filter(year >= min(emergence_select$brood_year)-1) |> 
  mutate(month_day = format(date, "%m-%d")) %>% 
  group_by(month_day) %>% 
  mutate(
    life_stage2 = case_when(
      month_day >= format(incubation_start_full, "%m-%d") | month_day <= format(incubation_end_full, "%m-%d") ~ "incubation",
      yday > 100 & yday < 122 ~ "fry migration",
      yday > 121 & yday < 214 ~ "rearing",
      yday > 212 & yday < 260 ~ "rearing",
      yday > 158 & yday < 289 ~ "spawning"
    )
  ) |> 
  mutate(life_stage2 = factor(life_stage2, levels = c("incubation", "fry migration", "rearing", "adult migration", "spawn"), ordered = TRUE)) %>% 
  ungroup()

flow %>% 
  filter(life_stage2 %in% c("incubation", "fry migration")) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value))+
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(5, 28.3), lty = 2)+
  geom_point(size = 0.1)+
  facet_wrap(~life_stage2)+
  ylab("flow rate m3/s")+
  xlab("")+
  scale_color_discrete(guide = "none")+
  scale_y_log10()

scour_des <- flow %>% 
  filter(life_stage2 %in% c("incubation", "fry migration")) %>% 
  group_by(date) %>% 
  mutate(scour = max(c(value - 28.5, 0)), desiccation = max(c(5 - value, 0))) %>% 
  ungroup() |> 
  mutate(year = year(date)) |> 
  mutate(brood_year = ifelse(yday < 200, year - 1, year))

scour_des_sum <- scour_des %>% 
  group_by(brood_year, life_stage2) %>% 
  summarise(non_range_days = sum(scour > 0) + sum(desiccation>0),
            total_scour = sum(scour), 
            total_desiccation = sum(desiccation), 
            flow_mean = mean(value), 
            flow_max = max(value), 
            flow_min = min(value), 
            flow_median = median(value), n = n()) %>% 
  group_by(life_stage2) %>% 
  mutate(max_n = max(n)) %>% 
  filter(n > max_n-2) %>% 
  select(-n, -max_n) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(year = brood_year + 1)

freshet_mat <- flow %>% 
  filter(year %in% unique(emergence_select$brood_year)) %>% 
  mutate(month = month(date)) |> 
  filter(month < c(10)) %>% 
  select(year, yday, value) %>% 
  group_by(yday) %>% 
  mutate(nyears = n()) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  filter(nyears == length(unique(emergence_select$brood_year))) %>% 
  select(-nyears) %>% 
  spread(key = yday, value = value) %>% 
  select(-year) %>% 
  data.matrix()

env.df <- env.df %>% left_join(scour_des_sum %>% filter(life_stage2 == "incubation") %>% select(year, non_range_days, total_scour, total_desiccation))

emergence_select <- left_join(emergence_select |> mutate(date = as.Date(date)), flow |> 
  select(date, daily_flow = value)) |> 
  mutate(volume_m3 = ifelse(volume_m3 == 0, NA, volume_m3))
```

```{r thermal_barrier, include = FALSE}
barrier_thresh <- 22

thermal_barrier <- read.csv("../../Ok_sock_lifecycle_model/outputs/thermal_barrier.csv") %>% 
  select(-X) %>% 
  mutate(fry_year = year + 1) |> 
  mutate(onset_md = format(as.Date(as.Date(onset - 1, origin = "2020-01-01"), origin = "1970-01-01"), "%b %d")) |> 
  filter(threshold == barrier_thresh)

therm_mod <- lm(duration ~ onset, data = thermal_barrier)
thermal_barrier$duration_resid <- thermal_barrier$duration - predict(therm_mod)

ggplot(thermal_barrier |> mutate(onset = as.Date(onset - 1, origin = "2020-01-01")), aes(x = year, y = onset))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x = "", y = "Thermal barrier onset")+

ggplot(thermal_barrier, aes(x = year, y = duration))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x = "", y = "Thermal barrier duration (days)")+
  
  ggplot(thermal_barrier |> mutate(onset = as.Date(onset - 1, origin = "2020-01-01")), aes(x = onset, y = duration))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = year)) +
  labs(x = "Thermal barrier onset",  y = "Thermal barrier duration (days)",)+
  
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")


env.df <- env.df %>% 
  left_join(thermal_barrier |> select(-year), by = c("year" = "fry_year"))

#get air temperatures near Malott for imputation
malott_air <- meteo_pull_monitors(
  monitors = "USW00094197",
  date_min = as.Date(paste(min(env.df$year)-1,06,01,sep = "-"), format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
  date_max = as.Date(paste(max(env.df$year),08,30,sep = "-"), format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
  var = c("TMAX","TMIN")
)

malott_air <- malott_air |> 
  mutate(air_mean = ((tmax + tmin)/2)/10) |> 
  mutate(month = month(date), year = year(date), yday = yday(date))


malott_june_air <- malott_air |> filter(month == 6) |>
  filter(!is.na(air_mean)) |> 
  group_by(year) |> 
  summarise(june_malott_air = mean(air_mean)) |> 
  mutate(fry_year = year+1)

left_join(thermal_barrier, malott_june_air) |> 
ggplot(aes(x = june_malott_air, y = onset - min(onset)+1))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = year))+
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm')+
  scale_y_log10()

env.df <- env.df %>% 
  left_join(malott_june_air |> select(-year), by = c("year" = "fry_year"))
```

```{r stan, include = FALSE}
dayV <- seq(min(emergence_select$yday)-3, max(emergence_select$yday)+5)

emergence_select <- emergence_select |> 
  filter(sample_year != 2018)  #2018 surveys seem to have used very different timing (many sets early in the day) and all finished before 10PM

enf.df<- env.df |> 
  filter(brood_year>= min(emergence_select$brood_year), brood_year<=max(emergence_select$brood_year))
  
dat_list <- list(Y = length(unique(env.df$year)),
                 N = nrow(emergence_select),
                 D = length(dayV),
                 year = as.numeric(emergence_select$sample_year - min(emergence_select$sample_year)+1),
                 fry_obs = emergence_select$total_catch,
                 N_missing_volume = sum(is.na(emergence_select$volume_m3)),
                 volume_missidx = which(is.na(emergence_select$volume_m3)),
                 volume = ifelse(!is.na(emergence_select$volume_m3), emergence_select$volume_m3, -999),
                 sample_flow = emergence_select$daily_flow,
                 soak_time = emergence_select$soak_time_min,
                 day = emergence_select$yday - min(emergence_select$yday) + 1,
                 hour = stand(log(emergence_select$time_set_numeric)),
                 #new_moon_date = stand(env.df$new_moon_yday),
                 
                 exceeded_FWMT = as.numeric(env.df$non_range_days>0),
                 day_std = (dayV - mean(emergence_select$yday))/sd(emergence_select$yday),
                 spawner_ln_est = env.df$spawners_ln_est,
                 spawner_ln_sd = env.df$spawner_ln_sd,
                 
                 N_missing_ATU = sum(is.na(env.df$ATU)),
                 ATU_missidx = which(is.na(env.df$ATU)),
                 ATU = ifelse(!is.na(env.df$ATU), stand(env.df$ATU), -999),
                 
                 N_missing_thermal = sum(is.na(env.df$onset)),
                 thermal_missidx = which(is.na(env.df$onset)),
                 thermal_onset = ifelse(!is.na(env.df$onset), env.df$onset, -999),
                 onset_mean = mean(env.df$onset, na.rm = TRUE),
                 onset_sd = sd(env.df$onset, na.rm = TRUE),
                 onset_low_bound = min(env.df$onset, na.rm = TRUE),
                 
                 thermal_dur_resid = ifelse(!is.na(env.df$duration_resid), env.df$duration_resid/sd(env.df$duration_resid, na.rm = TRUE), -999),
                 
                 malott_june_air = stand(env.df$june_malott_air),
                 
                 freshet_days = ncol(freshet_mat),
                 freshet_flow = freshet_mat,
                 freshet_threshold = 50,
                 freshet_transition_slope = 0.2,

                 sigma_sf_prior = 1,
                 beta_sf_prior = 0,
                 alpha_sf_prior = -1, #-3
                 beta_sf_sigma_prior = 1, #0.5,
                 alpha_sf_sigma_prior = 1
)

init_year <- min(emergence_select$sample_year) - 1

stan_file <- "../code/stan/emergence_skew_h.stan"
fit <- run_or_load_model(
  model_name = "emerge_m",
  stan_path = stan_file,
  data_list = dat_list, 
  cache_dir = "../model_fits",
  chains = 4, 
  threads_per_chain = 1,
  iter_sampling = 1000,
  iter_warmup = 1000,

# Abstract
Okanagan sockeye salmon have shown a recovery over the past three decades, but the relative contributions of environmental conditions and management actions are unclear. We developed a hierarchical Bayesian model linking spawner‑to‑fry productivity, fry emergence phenology, and sampling observations to evaluate how flow and temperature during adult upstream migration and incubation influence productivity. Productivity declined by `r -round(median(fry_percent_change$barrier_combined))`% in years with earlier onset and longer duration of periods when warm river temperatures created barriers to adult migration, indicating that migration conditions can have carry over effects on reproductive success even when spawners successfully reach the spawning grounds. Similarly, productivity was `r -round(median(fry_percent_change$FWMT))`% lower when flows fell outside a management target range designed to minimize scour and desiccation during egg incubation. In contrast, we found little support for effects of pre-spawning flows or incubation temperature on productivity. These findings provide quantitative evidence that current flow management is increasing freshwater production and has likely contributed to the Okanagan sockeye recovery. Effective flow management may therefore help offset climate driven impacts that increasingly threaten this population.

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} salmon; Oncorhynchus; spawner; fry; temperature; flow; incubation; Osoyoos Lake; Okanagan River; Columbia River

\newpage

# Introduction
Sockeye salmon (*Oncorhynchus nerka*) populations are in decline over much of their southern range in North America [@rand2012; @grant2019], highlighting the urgent need for management measures that can boost survival and contribute to maintenance and recovery. In this context, the Okanagan sockeye represent a rare success story where targeted management measures have proven effective [@alexander2024], resulting in a twentyfold increase in spawner abundance since the early 2000s [@bailey2025]. However, because multiple management measures were implemented concurrently---including habitat restoration, hatchery restocking, improved dam passage, and management of dam outflows to ensure “fish‑friendly flows”---alongside changing environmental conditions, it has proven challenging to quantify the contribution of individual interventions. Based on a weight of evidence approach, @alexander2024 concluded that these management interventions jointly contributed to the recovery, and amplified the positive effects of a 2007 shift towards more favourable coastal marine conditions. Still, quantitative estimates of how environmental conditions and individual management interventions impact productivity and survival are needed in order to ensure that limited conservation resources are used effectively, and to assess whether similar interventions could support recovery in other salmon populations. 

This study focuses on the spawner-to-fry component of the Okanagan sockeye life cycle, with the goal of quantifying how environmental conditions and management interventions influence production at this stage. Sockeye spawn in autumn when they lay their eggs in pockets (i.e., redds) in the gravel of streams, and these eggs incubate over the winter, hatching into alevins, before emerging as fry in the spring [@wilson2025]. Productivity during this life stage may be influenced by the number of spawning adults and their condition, the condition of the spawning grounds, and environmental conditions during egg incubation. 

During the incubation period, high flows can scour the stream bed, potentially dislodging or burying eggs and alevins, while also increasing fine sediment infiltration, which in turn reduces oxygen supply [@devries1997; @ingram2011]. Conversely, if flows are low enough to expose the eggs to air, mortality can occur through desiccation or freezing [@casas-mulet2015]. While scouring flows during the incubation period can reduce survival, they may have beneficial effects if they occur at other times of year. Over time, fine sediments can accumulate in spawning habitat, filling the spaces between spawning gravels, and causing mortality by reducing dissolved oxygen and trapping emerging alevins [@moring1982]. High-velocity flows, such as those during freshet, can flush fine sediments from spawning gravel, and may be critical to maintaining productive spawning habitat [@reiser1989].

While desiccation, scour, and sediment flushing occur naturally, they are directly influenced by dam-regulated flow regimes, as is the case in the Okanagan River. Because of this, the Okanagan Basin Implementation Board adopted seasonally varying target flows in 1976, to ensure that flow is suitable for each life stage of salmon in the river [@okanaganbasinimplementationboard1982], but challenges associated with balancing flood mitigation as well as uncertainty in real-time conditions resulted in flows frequently exceeding or falling below this range [@ng2025]. To address this issue, the Fish/Water Management Tool (FWMT) was developed as a decision support tool that provides real-time predictions of the consequences of water management decisions for fish and other users [@hyatt2015]. Since its implementation in 2004, there have been fewer days where flows fell below or exceeded the target flow range [@ng2025; @alexander2024].

It has been assumed that improved flow compliance has reduced scour and desiccation, thereby improving egg-to-fry survival. However, quantifying this benefit is challenging due to limited fry abundance data prior to FWMT implementation. @ng2025 found that emerging fry recruitment (i.e., fry per spawner) was higher in the 19 years after the FWMT was implemented, compared to the three years prior. Similarly, @alexander2024 found a two-fold increase in the ratio of overwintering juveniles (in the fall and winter following emergence) to spawners after brood year 2008 (four years post FWMT implementation) and concluded that FWMT was a strong contributing factor to the sockeye recovery. Despite this, neither study was able to establish a causal link between fry recruitment and interannual variation in flow rates.

Temperatures experienced during incubation may influence spawner‑to‑fry production, with embryo survival declining at temperatures of 14-16$^{\circ}$C [@beacham1990; @whitney2013]. However, this range is considerably higher than those observed in the Okanagan River, which rarely exceed 10$^{\circ}$C during incubation. Thus, it remains unclear whether interannual variation in incubation temperatures affects survival of Okanagan sockeye.

Beyond the direct effects of incubation conditions, upstream migration conditions may indirectly influence spawner‑to‑fry production through effects on spawner condition, separate from any effects on abundance due to migration mortality [@fenkes2016]. Elevated river temperatures place considerable stress on migrating sockeye; higher temperatures increase energy use [@rand2006], promote pathogen development [@crossin2008], and reduce aerobic scope [@eliason2011]. This results in reduced migration survival when temperatures exceed 18$^{\circ}$C [@martins2012], particularly for females [@crossin2008; @martins2012a]. There is also evidence that high temperatures encountered during migration lead to egg-retention [@quinn2007], reduced time on the spawning grounds [@minke-martin2018], and reduced egg-to-fry survival [@patterson2004], even when spawners are able to reach the spawning grounds. 

Okanagan sockeye begin their 830 km migration up the mainstem of the Columbia River in mid June, passing by nine hydroelectric dams and reaching the confluence of the Okanagan River (spelled Okanogan in the U.S.A.) by late June or early July. From there, they migrate an additional 185 km up the Okanagan River reaching their spawning grounds above Osoyoos Lake. Summer temperatures in the lower Okanagan River routinely present a thermal barrier to migration, forcing fish to hold in Lake Pateros at the confluence with the Columbia River and resulting in considerable thermal stress [@miller-saunders2024] and en-route mortality [@hyatt2020]. Observations of broodstock collected by the Okanagan Nation Alliance `r paste0("kł c", "p", "\u0313", "\u0259", "l", "k", "\u0313", " stim", "\u0313")` hatchery indicate that fish that were forced to hold in Lake Pateros for an extended period produced fewer eggs compared to fish that were transported past the thermal barrier and held in cooler hatchery waters (pers. comm. D. Stefanovic and T. Marsel, Okanagan Nation Alliance), despite documented negative effects of maternal hatchery holding on egg size [@sopinka2016]. It is therefore plausible that the timing and duration of the thermal barrier may impact the productivity of the fish that survive to reach the spawning grounds. 

Here we present a process‑based Bayesian model that estimates how flow velocity and temperature, during and preceding the incubation period, influence spawner‑to‑fry production of sockeye salmon in the Okanagan River. This model allows us to test the following hypotheses: (1) higher pre-spawning flows increase production by flushing fine sediments from spawning gravel; (2) production is reduced in years when incubation-period flows fall outside the FWMT target range ($5\text{–}28.5~\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s}$), reflecting increased scour and desiccation risk; (3) interannual variation in incubation temperature has limited effects on production because temperatures during incubation generally remain within ranges suitable for embryo survival; (4) production is reduced in years when the thermal barrier in the lower Okanagan forms earlier and lasts longer, through carry-over effects of thermal stress on spawner condition. By quantifying the benefits of flow management for salmon and the risks posed by warming temperatures, this work supports the continued application of the Fish/Water Management Tool and provides insight into how similar approaches may support the sustainable management of Okanagan sockeye and other salmon populations.


# Methods 
## Study system
### Salmon enumeration
### Spawners
Spawner abundance was estimated using a previously published Bayesian model fit to spawner enumeration surveys conducted by the Okanagan Nation Alliance (ONA) in the Okanagan River Index section between Osoyoos and Vaseux lakes [Fig. \ref{fig:map}\; @thompsoninreview]. That model accounts for observation error and repeated counts of individuals on the spawning grounds, producing annual posterior distributions of total spawner abundance. For the present analysis, we used the posterior mean and standard deviation of log spawner abundance as inputs to the spawner-to-fry recruitment model (described below), thereby propagating uncertainty from the spawner estimation process.

### Fry emergence
The ONA has conducted fry emergence surveys in the Okanagan River each spring (March–May) since `r min(emergence_select$sample_year)`; trial sampling in 2002 and 2003 was excluded because methods were not standardized. Samples were also excluded in 2018 (brood year 2017) because a different methodology was tried and the peak evening sampling window was not included. Sampling occurs approximately weekly early in the emergence period and increases to every 3–4 days during peak emergence, with reduced frequency thereafter.

Emerging fry are sampled at Vertical Drop Structure 13, which is located just below the main sockeye spawning grounds for the Osoyoos population (Fig. \ref{fig:map}). Emerging fry are sampled using a fyke net (1 $\times$ 2 ft opening; 5 mm stretch mesh) with typically four sets per night, each with a target soak time of 15 minutes. For each set, total fry catch, soak time, and set start time are recorded. Since 2008, a flow meter has been used to estimate the sampled water volume for each set. To reduce heterogeneity in sampling conditions (particularly in early years), our analysis only includes sets conducted between 21:00 and 01:00 with soak times between 5 and 20 minutes, and with sampled volume of at least 10 m$^3$.  

## Environmental covariates
### Upstream migration thermal barrier
Following @stiff2026, we define the thermal barrier period as the days between June 25 and September 30 when minimum daily water temperatures in the lower Okanagan River, measured in Malott Washington (USGS station 12447200), exceed `r barrier_thresh` $^{\circ}$C without a break of at least five days. Daily mean water temperature records were obtained from the U.S. Geological Survey National Water Information System (NWIS) using the dataRetrieval R package [@decicco2025]. Gaps in the Malott temperature record were filled using a linear mixed-effects model relating daily minimum temperatures at Malott to concurrent temperatures at Oroville (USGS station 12439500) and the Similkameen River (USGS station 12442500), with year-specific random intercepts and slopes for both predictor stations. Although river temperatures can exceed `r barrier_thresh` $^{\circ}$C before June 25th, we set this as the earliest barrier date because no more than 5% of the run has passed Wells dam (directly downstream) by that date in any of the past 25 years [@columbiariverdartcolumbiabasinresearchuniversityofwashington2025]. 

The onset date of the thermal barrier is the first day of this period and the duration is the number of days that the thermal barrier lasts. In years in which water temperatures never exceed `r barrier_thresh` $^{\circ}$C, we define the onset date as 10 days after the latest onset date observed in the dataset. This allowed us to have a continuous covariate for our models, rather than leaving onset date in these years as undefined. Duration is strongly negatively correlated with onset date (*r* = `r round(cor(thermal_barrier$onset, thermal_barrier$duration), 2)`), reflecting the fact that duration is likely to be longer when onset is early (Fig. \ref{fig:envfig}A-C). To separate these effects, we used residual duration rather than observed duration, calculated from a linear model of duration as a function of onset date, indicating whether a barrier lasted longer or shorter than expected for its onset.

Because water temperatures are not available prior to `r min(thermal_barrier$year)`, we treated thermal-barrier onset and residual duration as partially missing covariates and estimated them within the Bayesian spawner-to-fry recruitment model. For years with missing water temperature data, standardized onset date (mean = 0, SD = 1) was modelled as a linear function of mean June air temperature from the nearby NOAA station USW00094197. The regression coefficients and residual variance were estimated from years with observed onset, and onset dates in missing years were inferred under this fitted relationship and error distribution. Residual duration (scaled by its standard deviation) was also treated as partially missing and was estimated within the Bayesian model by assuming a skew‑normal distribution across years; missing values were inferred from this distribution.

### Pre-spawn flushing flows
We characterized pre‑spawn flushing conditions using daily discharge from the Okanagan River near Oliver (Water Survey of Canada station 08NM085) during January through September preceding each spawning season (Fig. \ref{fig:envfig}D). To summarize the extent to which flows were capable of mobilizing fine sediments within the spawning gravel, we constructed an annual flushing index:

$$\text{flush}_y = \sum_{d \in D_y}\text{logit}^{-1}(k_{\text{flush}} \cdot (Q_{y,d} - Q^*))$$

where $Q_{y,d}$ is the discharge on day $d$ in year $y$ and $D_y$ includes all days from January through September. The parameters $Q^*$ and $k_{\text{flush}}$ define how daily discharge is translated into a flushing intensity between 0 (no mobilization) and 1 (widespread mobilization), representing a gradual transition from negligible gravel movement at low flows to widespread mobilization at high flows. Summing across days allows flushing effects to accumulate over the year preceding spawning.

We selected values for these parameters based on observations of gravel mobility in the Okanagan River spawning grounds, which show that movement begins to occur at around 28 $\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s}$ (aligned with the FWMT upper threshold for incubation flows), with full movement occurring at around 70 $\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s}$ [@summitenvironmentalconsultantsltd.2002]. Thus, we set $Q^*$ at the discharge corresponding to the approximate midpoint of this transition (`r dat_list$freshet_threshold` $\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s}$), and $k_{\text{flush}}$ to control the steepness of the response so that flushing intensity increases smoothly from near zero to near one across the observed range of gravel movement.

### Incubation period flow and temperature
We define the incubation period as `r incubation_start` to `r incubation_end`. These dates are defined based on the date that spawners have typically arrived on the spawning grounds [@thompsoninreview] and just prior to when emerging fry have been most abundant in the emergence samples [@stockwell2020]. To estimate flow rates on the spawning grounds, we use daily flow rates in the Okanagan River near Oliver, which is monitored by the Water Survey of Canada (Station 08NM085) and data were extracted directly from the FWMT. This station is directly downstream of the spawning grounds where spawner enumeration and fry emergence sampling occurs (Fig. \ref{fig:map}). In each year, we calculate: 1) whether any incubation-day discharge fell outside the FWMT target range of $5\text{–}28.5~\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s}$, and 2) the accumulated thermal units (ATUs) at the end of the incubation period (i.e., `r incubation_end`; Fig. \ref{fig:envfig}E,F). ATUs were calculated as the cumulative sum of mean daily water temperatures over the incubation period for each brood year .

## Directed acyclic graph and overall model structure
The assumed causal pathways and observation structure are summarized in a directed acyclic graph (DAG\; Fig. \ref{fig:DAG}), which separates (1) annual spawner‑to‑fry production, (2) within‑year emergence phenology linking annual fry abundance to daily emergence intensity, and (3) the observation process linking daily emergence to set‑level catches via sampling effort and timing. The DAG guided the structure of our joint Bayesian model, which we describe in the subsequent sections. The model combines multiple submodels in a single joint likelihood implemented in Stan [@stan2024] and fit in R version `r getRversion()` [@rcoreteam2024] using cmdstanr [@gabry2024].

We used Microsoft 365 Copilot (GPT-5) as a tool to support Stan model development, including discussion of alternative model structures, generation of example code, and identification of potential causes of convergence issues. All AI-generated suggestions and code were reviewed, tested, and verified by the authors for logic and accuracy before incorporation into the analysis.

## Estimating a metric of yearly fry abundance
The goal of these surveys is to estimate the peak and end dates of emergence. However, they can also provide a relative index of total fry abundance in each year $\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}$. The index is relative because the proportion of all emerging fry that are sampled is unknown. This annual index of fry abundance is treated as a latent state representing the relative seasonal total of emerging fry. It is shared by both the emergence observation submodel and the spawner-to-fry recruitment submodel within a joint likelihood, as outlined in the subsequent sections. The emergence data inform $\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}$, while the recruitment submodel provides its expectation for this index as a function of spawner abundance and environmental covariates.

### Fry-emergence submodel
To specify the latent emergence process, we modelled fry emergence as a smooth, unimodal skew-normal function of seasonal timing expressed on the day-of-year scale, such that the total index of fry abundance within a given year ($\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}$) is distributed across the emergence season $\mathcal{D}$. We define $\mathcal{D}$ was the sequence of days between `r min(dayV)` and `r max(dayV)`, which corresponds to `r format(make_date(2026, 1, 1) + days(min(dayV) - 1), "%B %e")`--`r format(make_date(2026, 1, 1) + days(max(dayV) - 1), "%B %e")` in non-leap years. The total number of fry, as well as the seasonal penology, vary across years such that:

$$\hat{N}_{y,d}^{\text{fry}} = \hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}\frac{\exp(-\frac{1}{2}z_{y,d}^2)\Phi(\kappa_y z_{y,d})}{\sum_{d' \in \mathcal{D}}\exp(-\frac{1}{2}z_{y,d'}^2)\Phi(\kappa_y z_{y,d'})}, \hspace{1cm} z_{y,d} = \frac{d - d_y^\mu}{d_y^\sigma},$$


where $\hat{N}_{y,d}^{\text{fry}}$ is the expected emergence intensity on day $d$ in year $y$. The parameters $d_y^{\mu}$, $d_y^{\sigma}$, and $\kappa_y$ represent the peak timing, the spread of emergence across days, and the skew of the distribution in year $y$, modelled hierarchically across years (peak and skew on the linear scale; spread on the log scale). We also allowed interannual variation in peak timing to depend on incubation temperature conditions by modelling $d_y^\mu$ as a linear function of accumulated thermal units (ATUs). The function $\Phi(.)$ denotes the standard normal cumulative distribution function. We used standardized (mean = 0, sd = 1) day $d$ in the model. 

We evaluated alternative formulations of the seasonal emergence phenology, including (i) a model with time-invariant skew $\kappa$, and (ii) a symmetric Gaussian emergence function. The skew-normal model with interannual variation in skew presented above had substantially improved out of sample predictive performance, as quantified using leave-one-out cross validation ($\Delta$ELPD > 49). 

We linked the latent emergence intensity to the observed fry counts from individual sets using a negative binomial likelihood with an overdispersion parameter $\phi^{\text{fry}}$. Thus, the observed fry count in set $i$ is modelled as:

$$N_i^{\text{fry}_{\text{obs}}} \sim \text{NegativeBinomial}(\mu^{\text{fry}}_i, \phi^{\text{fry}}),$$
with an expected value

$$\mu^{\text{fry}}_i = \exp\left( \log \hat{N}_{y_i, d_i}^{\text{fry}} + \beta^{V} \cdot (\log(V_i) - \log(100)) - \frac{(h_i - h^{\mu})^2}{2 (h^{\sigma})^2} \right).$$
Here, $\beta^{V}$ is the rate at which fry abundance increases with sampled volume $V_i$, expressed relative to 100 m$^3$. Within-day variation in emergence is modelled at the observation level using a unimodal Gaussian kernel on standardized log-transformed hours elapsed since 10:00 ($h_i$); sample times range from 21:00 to 01:00. Log-transforming elapsed sampling time captures the empircally observed log-normal pattern of fry abundance over the course of the evening (Fig. \ref{fig:frysetshour}) and substantially improves out of sample predictive performance, as quantified using leave-one-out cross validation ($\Delta$ELPD = 30.3). The parameter $h^{\mu}$ is the hour of peak emergence in the day, and $h^{\sigma}$ is the spread of emergence across hours in a day. 

Missing sampled volume was imputed jointly within the full Bayesian model using a lognormal regression of sampled volume on soak time and daily flow (both log-transformed). The parameters were estimated based on the observed volumes, and missing values were imputed based on these relationships. 


### Spawner-to-fry recruitment submodel  
We modelled expected fry abundance $\mu_y^{\text{sf}}$ in year $y$ as a Shepherd function [@shepherd1982] of spawner abundance $N_y^{\text{spawners}}$:

$$\mu_y^{\text{sf}} = \frac{\alpha_y^{\text{sf}} \cdot p_y^{\text{eff}} \cdot N_y^{\text{spawners}}}{1 + (\beta_y^{\text{sf}} \cdot N_y^{\text{spawners}}/10^5)^{\theta^{\text{sf}}}},$$
where $\alpha_y^{\text{sf}}$ is the density-independent production rate in year $y$, $\beta_y^{\text{sf}}$ is the rate of density dependence, and $\theta^{\text{sf}}$ governs the shape of density dependence. $p_y^{\text{eff}}$ is a proportional scaling factor that reduces the effective reproductive contribution of each spawner, based on thermal conditions experienced during upstream migration (see below). This spawner-to-fry recruitment function reduces to the Beverton-Holt [@beverton1957] form when $\theta^{\text{sf}}=1$ and approaches a Ricker [@ricker1954] form when $\theta^{\text{sf}}\to\infty$. Thus, it is a generalized version that does not assume a specific shape for density dependence. We divide $N_y^{\text{spawners}}$ by $10^5$ in the denominator to keep $\beta_y^{\text{sf}}$ near one, avoiding the need for very small parameter values.

### Density-independent productivity during incubation
We allow the density-independent production rate $\alpha_y^{\text{sf}}$ to vary from year-to-year based on environmental conditions experienced during incubation, modelling it as a log-linear function in order to ensure positivity:

$$\log \alpha_y^{\text{sf}} = \alpha_0^{\text{sf}} + \beta^{\text{FWMT}} \cdot \text{FWMT}_y + \beta^{\text{ATU}} \cdot \text{ATU}_y.$$
The parameter $\alpha_0^{\text{sf}}$ is the density-independent production rate during average conditions and the $\beta$ coefficients are the slope parameters that estimate the effect of whether or not discharge exceeded the FWMT target range at any point during the incubation period ($\beta^{\text{FWMT}}$) and accumulated thermal units during incubation ($\beta^{\text{ATU}}$).

### Thermal barrier impacts on per-capita spawner effectiveness
We model the effect of thermal conditions during upstream migration on spawner-to-fry production as a reduction in per-capita spawner reproductive effectiveness. We use a logistic function to represent this effect, reflecting the assumption that delayed thermal-barrier onset can increase effectiveness only up to the point at which all returning salmon have successfully migrated, beyond which additional delays confer no further benefit:

$$p_y^{\text{eff}} = \text{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_0^{\text{eff}} +\beta^{\text{onset}} \cdot \text{onset}_y + \beta^{\text{dur}} \cdot \text{dur}_y),$$ 
where $\alpha_0^{\text{eff}}$ represents baseline per-capita spawner effectiveness on the logit scale under average conditions, $\beta^{\text{onset}}$ describes the effect of thermal-barrier onset date, and $\beta^{\text{dur}}$ is the additional effect of barrier duration beyond that explained by onset timing. 

### Density dependence and pre-spawn flushing
We assume that density dependence during spawner-to-fry recruitment occurs primarily through crowding on the spawning grounds. As spawner abundance increases, there is greater competition for suitable spawning sites. This pushes spawners onto suboptimal gravel and can lead to superimposition, whereby later-arriving spawners build their redds on top of those built by earlier-arriving fish, reducing egg survival through disturbance and displacement [@burgner1969; @essington2000]. Thus, we assume that the effects of pre-spawn flushing of fine sediments should impact the population by changing the amount and quality of available spawning gravel [@moring1982; @reiser1989]. 

We modelled annual variation in density dependence as a function of the flushing index defined above. Specifically, we allowed the density-dependence parameter to vary log-linearly with the standardized flushing index:
$$\log \beta_y^{\text{sf}} = \beta_0^{\text{sf}} + \beta^{\text{flush}} \cdot \left(\frac{\text{flush}_y}{\operatorname{sd}(\text{flush})}\right).$$


### Process error and spawner uncertainty
We assume that the annual fry abundance index $\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}$ deviates from its expected value $\mu_y^{\text{sf}}$ due to process error $\sigma_{\text{proc}}^{\text{sf}}$, with log abundance following a normal distribution around the expected value:

$$\log \hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}} \sim \text{Normal}(\log \mu_y^{\text{sf}}, \sigma_{\text{proc}}^{\text{sf}}).$$
To propagate uncertainty in spawner abundance from our prior model [@thompsoninreview], we model log spawner abundance $\log N_y^{\text{spawners}}$ as a latent variable:

$$\log N_y^{\text{spawners}} \sim \text{Normal}(\hat{\mu}_y^{\text{spawners}}, \hat{\sigma}_y^{\text{spawners}})$$

where $\hat{\mu}_y^{\text{spawners}}$ and $\hat{\sigma}_y^{\text{spawners}}$ are the mean and standard deviation of log spawner abundance in a given year in that model. Full prior specifications for all parameters in the model are provided in Table \ref{tab:priorstable}.

## Quantifying environmental impacts on spawner-to-fry production
We estimated scenario-based contrasts in predicted fry production by varying each environmental covariate while holding all others at their mean value. Except when estimating its effect, the FWMT incubation flow rate range was assumed to be maintained. Predictions were generated at the median observed spawner abundance over the study period. For each contrast, fry production was estimated with the focal variable set to the `r low*100`% (low or short) and `r high*100`% (high or long) quantiles of its observed distribution. For the FWMT effect, we compared scenarios where incubation flows were maintained within the FWMT range (i.e., $\text{FWMT}_y = 0$) throughout the incubation period and where the flow exceeded this range at least once during incubation (i.e., $\text{FWMT}_y = 1$). For each posterior draw, we calculated the percent difference between scenarios. Percent change was calculated using the scenario with higher median predicted fry production as the reference state, such that all estimates are expressed as reductions in spawner-to-fry production.

## MCMC Chains
We ran four parallel Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains for 2000 iterations each, discarding the first 1000 as warm up. We assessed convergence using the rank-normalized version of the Gelman-Rubin diagnostic [@vehtari2021], and all parameters showed good convergence ($\hat{R} \le$ `r round(max(rhat_df$rhat), 3)`), with `r round(mean(rhat_df$rhat < 1.01) * 100, 1)`\% of $\hat{R}$ values below 1.01.

# Results
```{r emergecalc,  include = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
emerge_timing_summary <- spread_draws(fit, day_peak[year], day_sd[year], day_skew[year]) %>% 
  mutate(brood_year = init_year + year - 1) %>%
  mutate(day_peak = day_peak * sd(emergence_select$yday) + mean(emergence_select$yday),
         day_sd = day_sd * sd(emergence_select$yday)) |> 
  group_by(brood_year) |> 
  summarise(day_peak = median(day_peak), day_sd = median(day_sd), day_skew = median(day_skew)) |> 
  mutate(day_peak_string = format(make_date(2026, 1, 1) + day_peak - 1, "%B %e"))

ws <- as_draws_df(fit$draws("emerge_phenology_L_corr"))

extract_corr <- function(row) {
  L <- matrix(0, 3, 3)
  L[lower.tri(L, diag = TRUE)] <- as.numeric(row)
  C <- L %*% t(L)
  c(C[1,2], C[1,3], C[2,3])
}

corr_mat <- t(apply(ws, 1, extract_corr))

colnames(corr_mat) <- c("peak_sd", "peak_skew", "sd_skew")

summary_corr <- function(x) {
  c(
    median = median(x),
    lower = unname(quantile(x, 0.025)),
    upper = unname(quantile(x, 0.975))
  )
}
```
## Fry emergence
Fry emergence abundance and timing varied among brood years (Fig. \ref{fig:fryemergefig}). The fry abundance index ranged from `r round(fry_abund_summary$fry_ind[which(fry_abund_summary$fry_ind == min(fry_abund_summary$fry_ind))])` in brood year `r round(fry_abund_summary$brood_year[which(fry_abund_summary$fry_ind == min(fry_abund_summary$fry_ind))])` to `r format(round(fry_abund_summary$fry_ind[which(fry_abund_summary$fry_ind == max(fry_abund_summary$fry_ind))]), scientific = FALSE, big.mark = "\u2009")` in brood year `r round(fry_abund_summary$brood_year[which(fry_abund_summary$fry_ind == max(fry_abund_summary$fry_ind))])` (Fig. \ref{fig:fryemergefig}B). 

Peak emergence timing ($d_y^{\mu}$) ranged from `r emerge_timing_summary$day_peak_string[which(emerge_timing_summary$day_peak== min(emerge_timing_summary$day_peak))]` in brood year `r emerge_timing_summary$brood_year[which(emerge_timing_summary$day_peak== min(emerge_timing_summary$day_peak))]` to `r emerge_timing_summary$day_peak_string[which(emerge_timing_summary$day_peak== max(emerge_timing_summary$day_peak))]` in brood year `r emerge_timing_summary$brood_year[which(emerge_timing_summary$day_peak== max(emerge_timing_summary$day_peak))]` (Fig. \ref{fig:fryemergefig}C). Peak emergence timing ($d_y^{\mu}$) occurred earlier in years with higher accumulated thermal units during the incubation period (Fig. \ref{fig:timingATU}), with full posterior support for a negative relationship. 

The width of the emergence window (i.e., number of days over which 95% of emergence occurred) varied from as short as `r min(emergence_window_summary$days95)` days in brood year `r emergence_window_summary$brood_year[which(emergence_window_summary$days95 == min(emergence_window_summary$days95))]` to as long as `r max(emergence_window_summary$days95)` days in brood year `r emergence_window_summary$brood_year[which(emergence_window_summary$days95 == max(emergence_window_summary$days95))]` (Fig. \ref{fig:fryemergefig}D). The parameters describing emergence timing were correlated. In years with later peak timing ($d_y^{\mu}$), emergence windows tended to be broader (r = `r round(summary_corr(corr_mat[, "peak_sd"])["median"], 2)`, 95% CrI: `r round(summary_corr(corr_mat[, "peak_sd"])["lower"], 2)` to `r round(summary_corr(corr_mat[, "peak_sd"])["upper"], 2)`) while skew tended to decrease with later peak timing (r = `r round(summary_corr(corr_mat[, "peak_skew"])["median"], 2)`, 95% CrI: `r round(summary_corr(corr_mat[, "peak_skew"])["lower"], 2)` to `r round(summary_corr(corr_mat[, "peak_skew"])["upper"], 2)`; Fig. \ref{fig:fryemergefig}A).


## Drivers of spawner-to-fry production
Relative fry abundance increased with spawner abundance in a density-dependent manner (Fig. \ref{fig:fryspawnfig}). The shape of this recruitment relationship was consistent with Beverton-Holt type compensation, with no evidence of overcompensation (i.e., $\theta^{\text{sf}} \sim 1$; Fig. \ref{fig:pprecruitment}). There were substantial yearly deviations from the average recruitment relationship, with thermal barrier dynamics and river discharge during incubation identified as the strongest drivers (Fig. \ref{fig:fryspawnfig}B).

When the thermal barrier begins early (`r format(as.Date(as.Date(quantile(thermal_barrier$onset, low) - 1, origin = "2020-01-01"), origin = "1970-01-01"), "%B %d")`) and persists for a long duration, fry production was estimated to change by approximately `r round(median(fry_percent_change$barrier_combined))`\% (95\% CrI: `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$barrier_combined, 0.025))`\% to `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$barrier_combined, 0.975))`\%) relative to years with late onset (`r format(as.Date(as.Date(quantile(thermal_barrier$onset, high) - 1, origin = "2020-01-01"), origin = "1970-01-01"), "%B %d")`) and short duration, with a `r round(mean(fry_percent_change$barrier_combined < 0) * 100)`\% probability of a negative effect (Fig. \ref{fig:fryspawnfig}C). This combined effect was larger than the estimated effects of any other environmental driver and was primarily the result of variation in barrier onset date. When the thermal barrier begins early, fry production was estimated to change by approximately `r round(median(fry_percent_change$onset))`\% relative to a late onset (95\% CrI: `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$onset, 0.025))`\% to `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$onset, 0.975))`\%), with a `r round(mean(fry_percent_change$onset < 0) * 100)`\% probability of a negative effect. After accounting for variation in onset date, the estimated effect of duration was weaker, with long versus short thermal barrier duration changing fry production by `r round(median(fry_percent_change$dur))`\% (95\% CrI: `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$dur, 0.025))`\% to `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$dur, 0.975))`\%), with a `r round(mean(fry_percent_change$dur < 0) * 100)`\% probability of a negative effect. 

Fry production in years with low pre-spawn flushing was estimated to differ by `r round(median(fry_percent_change$freshet))`% relative to years with high flushing (95\% CrI: `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$freshet,0.025))`\% to `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$freshet, 0.975))`\%), with a `r round(mean(fry_percent_change$freshet<0) * 100)`% probability of a negative effect. When flows during the incubation period fall outside of the target range from the FWMT $(5\text{–}28.5~\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s})$, fry production was estimated to change by `r round(median(fry_percent_change$FWMT))`\% (95\% CrI: `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$FWMT, 0.025))`\% to `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$FWMT, 0.975))`\%), with a `r round(mean(fry_percent_change$FWMT < 0) * 100)`\% probability of a negative effect. 

In years with low incubation accumulated thermal units, fry production was estimated to differ by `r round(median(fry_percent_change$ATU))`\% relative to years with high incubation accumulated thermal units (95\% CrI: `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$ATU, 0.025))`\% to `r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$ATU, 0.975))`\%), with a `r round(mean(fry_percent_change$ATU < 0) * 100)`\% probability of a negative effect.

# Discussion
Our analysis shows that spawner-to-fry production is strongly influenced by thermal barrier dynamics and whether flows during incubation remain within the FWMT target range. In contrast, neither pre-spawning flows nor incubation temperature meaningfully influence production, despite the strong influence of temperature on emergence timing. These results are consistent with thermal barrier dynamics influencing production through carry‑over effects on spawner condition, and with incubation flow conditions influencing egg and embryo survival through scouring and desiccation. These findings highlight the growing risk posed by climate warming during the upstream migration stage through its effects on thermal barrier dynamics. They also provide evidence that managing flows using the FWMT benefits fry production, suggesting that effective flow management may partially offset climate‑related impacts on freshwater production.

While the effects of the Okanagan River thermal barrier on migration delay and survival of returning sockeye are well documented [@hyatt2020; @murauskas2021], our analysis suggests that it is also a major driver of spawner-to-fry production. We estimate that productivity is approximately `r -round(median(fry_percent_change$barrier_combined))`% lower in years with early-onset, long-duration thermal barriers than in years with late-onset, short-duration barriers. This combined effect was driven primarily by variation in barrier onset date, although longer barrier duration contributed additional reductions in production after accounting for onset. These impacts likely arise from the physiological stress associated with holding and migrating through warm water [@eliason2011; @fenkes2016], representing a carry-over effect from the adult migration stage to fry production [@gosselin2021]. This is consistent with the observations from the Okanagan Nation Alliance hatchery, where reduce egg mass and number were found in fish that experienced prolonged holding below the thermal barrier (pers. comm. D. Stefanovic and T. Marsel, Okanagan Nation Alliance). Our analysis does not allow us to distinguish which aspects of spawner condition are affected, but previous work suggests that elevated temperatures can influence reproductive success through increased egg retention [@quinn2007], increased pathogen development [@crossin2008], and reduced egg-to-fry survival [@patterson2004]. 

Although the thermal barrier in the Okanagan River has been documented since the 1960s [@murauskas2021], it now occurs more frequently, with earlier onset and longer duration [@hyatt2020], and is projected to intensify under climate change, shifting from an episodic occurrence to a chronic constraint on migration [@stiff2026]. As a result, the Okanagan River thermal barrier represents a key bottleneck in the life cycle that may pose a risk to the long‑term viability of Okanagan sockeye. 

Our analysis finds that spawner‑to‑fry production is higher when Okanagan River flows remain within the FWMT target range of $5\text{–}28.5~\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s}$ during the incubation period. Production was estimated to be approximately `r round(-median(fry_percent_change$FWMT))`% lower in years when flows fell outside the target range, corresponding to an increase of approximately `r round(median(fry_percent_change$FWMT_benefit))`% when flows remained within it. This result provides quantitative support for the effectiveness of the FWMT, consistent with its design to minimize mortality from both scour at high discharge and desiccation at low discharge [@hyatt2015]. Previous studies documented increases in fry and pre-smolt production following FWMT implementation [@ng2025; @alexander2024], but were unable to link these changes directly to interannual variation in flow conditions. Our results suggest that improved compliance with the target flow range is the likely mechanism underlying these patterns, underscoring the value of flow management as a tool for supporting freshwater production. 

In contrast, we find limited support for the hypotheses that pre-spawning flows and incubation temperature influence spawner-to-fry production, with weak directional effects and credible intervals overlapping zero. The limited support for effects of pre-spawning flows may reflect that sediment flushing has a relatively small influence on fry production in this system. Alternatively, the flushing index used here may not fully capture the relationship between discharge and sediment mobilization. However, because it is based on empirical observations of gravel mobilization in the Okanagan River [@summitenvironmentalconsultantsltd.2002], substantial mischaracterization of flushing conditions is unlikely. The limited support for effects of incubation temperature is consistent with previous empirical evidence showing that negative impacts of temperature on embryo survival occur at higher temperatures than those experienced in the Okanagan River [@beacham1990; @whitney2013]. 

The structure of our model was guided by an explicit causal framework represented in our DAG (Fig. \ref{fig:DAG}), which makes transparent the assumed links between observed data and underlying processes and provides a structured basis for evaluating causal mechanisms [@pearl2016; @mcelreath2020]. Nevertheless, the validity of our inference depends on the accuracy of these assumed relationships, as well as on the simplifying assumptions required to make the model tractable. In particular, we assume that our index of relative fry abundance provides a reasonable proxy for absolute fry abundance. We also assume that fry emergence can be adequately described using a skew-normal distribution over the season and a log-normal distribution within each evening. More generally, all environmental covariates in the model are represented using indices that approximate underlying processes rather than directly measuring them. For example, thermal barrier dynamics are represented using a $22\,^\circ$C threshold over the period from June 25 to September 30, which may not fully capture the spatial and temporal variability in thermal exposure experienced by migrating fish. Finally, the relationships specified in the DAG are implemented using specific functional forms, including Shepherd recruitment, which may not fully capture the true underlying relationships. 

These results provide important insight into the potential causes of the Okanagan sockeye salmon recovery by offering quantitative support for previously hypothesized links between environmental conditions, management actions, and spawner‑to‑fry production [@alexander2024]. In particular, our analysis supports the hypothesis that FWMT compliance has been an important contributor to the recovery. However, our results only demonstrate the benefits of the FWMT at a single life stage. To assess how these benefits persist through the sockeye life cycle and influence adult recruitment, integration into full life‑cycle models will be necessary. Despite this, our results suggest that management measures such as FWMT may help offset some factors that negatively impact survival, including dam passage-related mortality, the Okanagan River thermal barrier, and marine heat waves. Many of these stressors are expected to be exacerbated by climate change and are not easily managed [@connors2025; @thorstad2021]. In this context, by providing a quantitative assessment of FWMT effectiveness, our model also establishes a framework for reassessing its performance as additional data become available.

Although this analysis is grounded in the Okanagan system and the specific context of the FWMT, the underlying mechanisms have broader relevance for other salmon populations. Our findings highlight the benefits of limiting scour and desiccation during the incubation life stage; in systems where flows are actively managed, adopting fish‑friendly flow regimes would likely provide similar improvements in productivity. Even in systems without direct flow regulation, habitat restoration measures that reduce the frequency or intensity of extreme flow conditions may also increase fry production. Return migration temperatures are already a concern in other watersheds, even where temperatures do not consistently reach levels that fully impede migration [e.g., Fraser and Somass Rivers\; @eliason2011; @brown2026]. The impacts of the thermal barrier observed in the Okanagan River may therefore provide insight into the consequences of continued warming in these and other systems. Overall, these findings illustrate how targeted management measures such as the FWMT can help mitigate the negative effects of extreme environmental conditions, while potentially buffering salmon populations against some of the impacts of climate change. More broadly, they also highlight the value of quantitative, process‑based approaches for guiding adaptive management.

  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "",
    labels = function(y) format(as.Date(y, origin = "2020-01-01"), "%b %d"), expand = c(0, 0),
    breaks = seq(91, 121, length = 2)
  )+
  scale_colour_viridis_c("Hrs.\nafter\n8PM")+
  ylab("Fry per volume (m3)")
```

```{r frysetshour, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE,  fig.width=9, fig.height=6, fig.cap = "Observed fry per volume of water sampled over hours elapsed since 20:00. Sets are restricted to those between day-of-year 96 and 120, for visual clarity. Years are sample year (i.e, brood year + 1)."}
spread_draws(fit, volume_merge[set]) |> 
  group_by(set) |> 
  summarise(volume = median(volume_merge)) |> 
  mutate(fry = dat_list$fry_obs, year = dat_list$year, day = dat_list$day, hour = dat_list$hour) |> 
  mutate(yday = day + min(emergence_select$yday) - 1) |> 
  mutate(brood_year = year + init_year - 1) |> 
  mutate(sample_year = brood_year + 1) |> 
  mutate(hour = hour * sd(emergence_select$time_set_numeric) + mean(emergence_select$time_set_numeric)) |> 
  filter(yday>96, yday<120) |> 
ggplot(aes(x = hour, y = fry/volume, color = yday))+
  geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~sample_year)+
  scale_y_log10()+
  scale_color_viridis_c("day-of-year")+
    ylab("Fry per volume (m3)")+
  xlab("Hours after 8PM")
```

```{r timingATU, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE,  fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap = "Date of peak emergence timing vs. accumulated thermal units (ATUs) during the incubation period. "}
spread_draws(fit, day_peak[year]) %>% 
  mutate(year = init_year + year) %>%
  mutate(day_peak = day_peak * sd(emergence_select$yday) + mean(emergence_select$yday)) %>% 
  left_join(env_post |> select(-day_peak)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = ATU, y = day_peak))+
  # stat_lineribbon(data = moon_emerge.df, aes(x = moon_day, y = day_peak, color = NULL, year = NULL), .width = c(CrIs))+
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, lty = 2)+
  stat_pointinterval(.width = CrIs, aes(group = year))+
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Greys", guide = "none")+
  #geom_text_repel(data = env_post, aes(label = year, y = day_peak_median), color = "dodgerblue2")+
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Estimated peak emergence date",
    labels = function(y) format(as.Date(y, origin = "2020-01-01"), "%b %d")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "ATUs during incubation period"
  )

```{r priorpost, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
n_draws <- nrow(post)

get_par <- function(name) post[[name]]

param_priors <- list(
  
  # --- Recruitment ---
  list("alpha[0]^sf", exp(post$alpha0),
       exp(rnorm(n_draws, dat_list$alpha_sf_prior, dat_list$alpha_sf_sigma_prior)), TRUE),
  
  list("beta[0]^sf", exp(post$beta0),
       exp(rnorm(n_draws, dat_list$beta_sf_prior, dat_list$beta_sf_sigma_prior)), TRUE),
  
  list("theta^sf", post$theta_sf,
       rnorm(n_draws, 1, 0.1), FALSE),
  
  list("sigma[proc]^sf", post$sigma_sf,
       rexp(n_draws, dat_list$sigma_sf_prior), TRUE),
  
  # --- Environmental ---
  list("beta^FWMT", post$a_FWMT,
       rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  list("beta^ATU", post$sf_ATU,
       rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  list("beta^flush", post$b_freshet,
       rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  list("beta[peak]^ATU", post$b_ATU_peak,
       rnorm(n_draws, -0.2, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  # --- Effective spawners ---
  list("alpha[0]^eff", post$a_effective_spawners,
       rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.25), FALSE),
  
  list("w[eff]", post$thermal_barrier_transition_width_sd,
       rlnorm(n_draws, log(2.5), 0.5), TRUE),
  
  list("beta^onset", post$b_therm_onset_raw,
       rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  list("beta^dur", post$b_therm_dur_raw,
       rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  # --- Volume ---
  list("a[vol]", post$a_volume,
       rnorm(n_draws, 0, 1), FALSE),
  
  list("beta[soak]", post$soak_b,
       rnorm(n_draws, 1, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  list("beta[flow]", post$b_sample_flow,
       rnorm(n_draws, 1, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  list("sigma[vol]", post$sigma_volume,
       rlnorm(n_draws, log(0.3), 0.4), TRUE),
  
  list("beta^V", post$b_volume,
       rnorm(n_draws, 1, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  # --- Diel ---
  list("h^mu", post$hour_peak,
       rnorm(n_draws, -0.5, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  list("h^sigma", post$hour_sd,
       rlnorm(n_draws, log(1), 0.4), TRUE),
  
  # --- Emergence phenology ---
  list("mu[d]^mu", get_par("emerge_phenology_mu[1]"),
       rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  list("mu[d]^sigma", get_par("emerge_phenology_mu[2]"),
       rnorm(n_draws, -0.5, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  list("mu[d]^skew", get_par("emerge_phenology_mu[3]"),
       rnorm(n_draws, -2, 1), FALSE),
  
  list("sigma[d]^mu", get_par("emerge_phenology_sigma[1]"),
       rlnorm(n_draws, log(0.3), 0.4), TRUE),
  
  list("sigma[d]^sigma", get_par("emerge_phenology_sigma[2]"),
       rlnorm(n_draws, log(0.3), 0.4), TRUE),
  
  list("sigma[d]^skew", get_par("emerge_phenology_sigma[3]"),
       rlnorm(n_draws, log(2), 0.4), TRUE),
  
  list("phi^fry", post$emerg_phi,
       rlnorm(n_draws, log(5), 0.5), TRUE),
  
  # --- Onset ---
  list("a[onset]", post$a_onset,
       rnorm(n_draws, 0, 0.1), FALSE),
  
  list("beta[air]", post$b_air_onset,
       rnorm(n_draws, -0.5, 0.5), FALSE),
  
  list("sigma[onset]", post$onset_sigma,
       rexp(n_draws, 1), TRUE),
  
  # --- Duration ---
  list("xi[dur]", post$xi_dur,
       rnorm(n_draws, 0.5, 0.4), FALSE),
  
  list("omega[dur]", post$omega_dur,
       rnorm(n_draws, 1.3, 0.2), FALSE),
  
  list("alpha[dur]", post$alpha_dur,
       rnorm(n_draws, -2, 1), FALSE)
)

prior_post_df <- bind_rows(lapply(param_priors, function(p) {
  
  vals <- c(p[[2]], p[[3]])
  
  if (p[[4]]) {
    value_plot <- ifelse(vals > 0, log10(vals), NA)
  } else {
    value_plot <- vals
  }
  
  data.frame(
    value = vals,
    value_plot = value_plot,
    type = rep(c("Posterior", "Prior"), each = n_draws),
    parameter = p[[1]]
  )
}))

prior_post_df <- prior_post_df %>%
  mutate(group = case_when(
    
    parameter %in% c("alpha[0]^sf", "beta[0]^sf", "theta^sf", "sigma[proc]^sf") ~ "Recruitment",
    
    parameter %in% c("beta^FWMT", "beta^ATU", "beta^flush",
                     "beta[peak]^ATU", "beta^onset", "beta^dur") ~ "Environment",
    
    parameter %in% c("alpha[0]^eff", "w[eff]") ~ "Effective spawners",
    
    parameter %in% c("a[vol]", "beta[soak]", "beta[flow]",
                     "sigma[vol]", "beta^V", "h^mu", "h^sigma") ~ "Observation",
    
    parameter %in% c("mu[d]^mu", "mu[d]^sigma", "mu[d]^skew",
                     "sigma[d]^mu", "sigma[d]^sigma", "sigma[d]^skew",
                     "phi^fry") ~ "Phenology",
    
    parameter %in% c("a[onset]", "beta[air]", "sigma[onset]",
                     "xi[dur]", "omega[dur]", "alpha[dur]") ~ "Onset & duration"
    
  ))

plot_group <- function(df, grp_name) {
  ggplot(df %>% filter(group == grp_name),
         aes(x = value_plot, linetype = type)) +
    geom_density(size = 0.7, na.rm = TRUE) +
    facet_wrap(~ parameter, scales = "free", labeller = label_parsed) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(1, 2)) +
    theme_bw() +
    ggtitle(grp_name) +
    labs(x = "Parameter value", y = "Density")
}
```
